chapter_theme: The enemy worth having, seen coldly: pick the weak, and notice who makes himself easy to beat through anger, ignorance, stinginess and isolation. Read another way, its list of vices is a portrait of how not to become someone's easy enemy.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the general rule (861), the specific marks of a beatable foe (862-867), and the fruit of such enmity (868-870). The chapter never says it is addressed to the reader's own faults, but its catalogue works that way.

861.reading: Avoid opposing the strong, and without holding back, favour enmity against the weak.
861.nuance: Whatever this is, it is not a moral teaching, which is why the commentators' disagreement matters so much.

positions.position: It is a plain rule of statecraft: avoid the strong, and keep enmity with the weak, since beating them doesn't drain one's strength.
The weak in view are those who don't respect one, which narrows the rule.
The opposite: true excellence in enmity is leaving the weak alone and taking on the strong.
positions.quote: மெலியோரை விடுத்து, வலியோரை எதிர்த்துப் போரிட விரும்புவதே

862.reading: With no love, no worthy allies and no strength of his own, how can he wear down an enemy's might?
862.nuance: அன்பு appears in a list of military assets. For Parimelazhagar it is love of one's kin, so without it there's no kin, and for an attacker such a person only adds strength.

863.reading: He fears, doesn't know, doesn't fit in with others, doesn't give: he is utterly easy for an enemy.
863.nuance: The list includes not giving, which is an ethical failing elsewhere and here is a military one. Kalaignar's 'compassion' softens the word. Parimelazhagar says அஞ்சும் means fearing what needn't be feared, the mirror of 428.

864.reading: Not free from rage and without நிறை: at any time, in any place, he is easy for anyone.
864.nuance: The commentators differ on நிறை. Parimelazhagar means keeping secrets and Kalaignar means self-control. Parimelazhagar's logic is neat: the enemy no longer needs to watch for the right time, place or strength because the angry man's leaked plans give it all away.

865.reading: He doesn't look to the வழி, doesn't do what is suitable, doesn't look to blame, has no character: he is a pleasure to his enemies.

positions.position: வழி is the treatise on policy, handed down from the ancients, which he doesn't study.
வழி is the consequence of an action, which he doesn't consider when he starts it.
positions.quote: ஒருவினை செய்யத் தொடங்குங்கால் பின் வருவன பாரான்

866.reading: One of blinding anger and ever-growing lust: his not caring for you is something to care for.
866.nuance: பேணாமை பேணப்படும் is the wordplay and the whole point. Such a person's hostility is an asset, since he will destroy himself. Parimelazhagar says all become his enemies through the anger, and in the lust he loses sight of his affairs. Kalaignar turns காமம் into greed.

867.reading: One who stays close and does what is unbecoming: it is truly necessary to get his enmity, even by giving something.
867.nuance: Even the enmity has a price worth paying. The verse's hardest word is அடுத்திருந்து, and the commentators each supply a different object.

positions.position: He is a ruler who has begun a task and does what doesn't fit it, so losing a little to fight him pays many times over.
positions.quote: வினையைத் தொடங்கியிருந்து அதற்கு ஏலாதன செய்வான் பகைமையை

positions.position: He has taken up enmity and does what doesn't serve it, so he will not actually hurt you.
He is someone staying at your side and doing wrong, and you must pay to make him an open enemy.
positions.quote: தன்னோடு இருந்துகொண்டே தனக்குப் பொருந்தாத காரியங்களைச் செய்து கொண்டிருப்பவனைப்

868.reading: With no qualities and many faults he has no one around him, and this is a protection to his enemies.
868.nuance: ஏமாப்பு, the word for protection, has been turned around. A man's faults become his enemies' shield. Parimelazhagar lists what deserts him: kin, friends, wealth, army.

869.reading: Joy doesn't go far from those fighting, if they get enemies who are unknowing and afraid.
869.nuance: பெறின் sounds like luck. Parimelazhagar says that's because foes with neither knowledge nor resolve are rare.

870.reading: Fame will never come to one who cannot manage the small thing of being angry at the unlearned.
870.nuance: The syntax is hard and the commentaries don't converge. The reading given follows Parimelazhagar, who says others have not kept to the chapter's subject.

positions.position: Fighting the untaught is cheap in effort, and one who can't manage even that won't win fame.
positions.quote: நீதி அறியாதானை வேறல் எளிதாயிருக்கவும், அது மாட்டாதானை வெற்றியான் வரும் புகழ் கூடாது என்பதாம்

positions.position: The words describe one enemy who is unlearned, angry and poor, and it is he whom light never reaches.
positions.quote: கல்லாதானுமாய், வெகுளியுடையனுமாய், சிறு பொருளனுமாகிய பகைவனை எல்லா நாளும் ஒளி பொருந்தாது

links.note: The same two words, வலியார் and மெலியார், with opposite advice. 250 says that when going against the weak, remember how you stand before the strong, which is a brake. 861 tells a ruler to go against the weak with appetite. The Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth are at their furthest apart here.

Two adjacent chapter openings. 861 tells one to keep enmity with the weak. 871 says enmity shouldn't be desired even in jest. Parimelazhagar's way through is that 871 is about unworthy enmity (மாணாத பகை), but the verses don't draw this distinction.

The same phrase, கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும். 794 says to pay for the friendship of a person of honour. 867 says to pay for the enmity of a fool. The Kural prices enemies and friends in the same way, and both are investments.

source_issues: 869: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.
